evidence: Vulg. Mt. 6.28: Cōnsīderāte līlia agrī quōmodo crēscunt
Sen. Ep. 77.20: quōmodo fābula, sīc vīta
terms.comment: Often written as two words (Catull. 10.7). As a relative it answers sīc: quōmodo … sīc, as … so.

terms.gloss: how; in the way that, as
evidence: Plin. Ep. 9.36.1: quaeris, quemadmodum in Tuscīs diem aestāte dispōnam
Sen. Ep. 47.11: sīc cum īnferiōre vīvās quemadmodum tēcum superiōrem velīs vīvere
terms.comment: Mostly in indirect questions and in comparisons.

terms.grammar: adverb (an old ablative of quī, quis)
evidence: Phaedr. 1.1.7: quī possum, quaesō, facere quod quereris, lupe?
terms.comment: Above all in short questions of speech: quī scīs?, how do you know?; quī potest?, how can it be? (Lewis & Short).
Ut valēs?, how are you? (see “how are you?”).
Quam longē?, how far?; quam mox?, how soon?

phrases.latin: Cōnsīderāte līlia agrī quōmodo crēscunt: nōn labōrant, neque nent.
phrases.english: Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin.

phrases.latin: quī possum, quaesō, facere quod quereris, lupe?
phrases.english: how can I do what you complain of, wolf?

phrases.latin: quaeris, quemadmodum in Tuscīs diem aestāte dispōnam
phrases.english: you ask how I lay out my day in summer at my Tuscan place

phrases.latin: quōmodo fābula, sīc vīta: nōn quam diū, sed quam bene ācta sit, rēfert
phrases.english: as with a play, so with life: what matters is not how long but how well it has been acted

phrases.latin: quid esset jam Bīthȳnia, quō modō sē habēret
phrases.english: what Bithynia was like now, how it was getting on

phrases.latin: Salvē, anime mī. — Ō mī exspectāte, salvē. — Ut valēs? — Salvum advēnisse gaudeō.
phrases.english: Hello, my darling. — Oh, how I’ve waited for you, hello. — How are you? — I’m glad you’re home safe.
